intro: Key West's two remarkable trees are a champion you can eat and a pair the city has asked to cut down. Florida's largest mammee apple grows in the yard of the Key West Firehouse Museum in Old Town, its fruit goes into the museum's annual mamey ice cream social, and the museum puts it at 100 to 120 years old. In the city cemetery, two strangler figs have grown so far into the graves that the city's own foresters asked to remove them. In February 2026 that decision was postponed indefinitely.
meta_description: Florida's state champion mammee apple grows in the Key West Firehouse Museum yard, and its fruit becomes ice cream every year.
question_answer: We map two trees in Key West: the Firehouse Museum Mamey, Florida's state champion mammee apple, which the museum puts at somewhere between 100 and 120 years old, and the strangler figs of the Key West Cemetery, which the local paper calls over a century old. Neither has a planting record.
question_meta: Florida's champion mammee apple and the cemetery's strangler figs, both roughly a century old or more, in Old Town Key West. Where and when to see them.
question_context: The mamey stands on city land between the Key West Firehouse Museum and the building next door, at the corner of Grinnell and Virginia streets. In 2018 the county forester measured it at 328 centimetres round and 14.9 metres tall and recorded it as fair, mature and declining; it was still bearing fruit in June 2024. Its age is the museum's estimate, worked back from the roughly 21 years a mamey needs before it fruits. The museum is free, with a suggested donation, and opens Wednesday to Saturday from 10:00 to 14:00. The cemetery figs are over a century old by the local paper's account, though nobody has a planting date. The city measured them at 96 and 53 inches across, and its report shows them breaking and engulfing gravestones, most of them from the 1880s by a resident's account. The urban foresters asked to remove both in November 2025; residents objected, and the decision was postponed. We have not found where in the 19-acre cemetery they stand.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Key West?
faq.a: Nobody knows for certain. The Firehouse Museum Mamey is put at 100 to 120 years by the museum, and the strangler figs in the Key West Cemetery are called over a century old by the local paper. Neither has a planting record.

faq.q: Is the Firehouse Museum Mamey free to see?
faq.a: The museum is free, with a suggested donation of $5, and opens Wednesday to Saturday from 10:00 to 14:00, last admission 13:30.

faq.q: Are the Key West Cemetery figs being cut down?
faq.a: The city's urban foresters asked to remove both in November 2025. Residents objected, and by February 2026 the decision had been postponed indefinitely, with no vote since that we have found.

trees.story:
Florida's largest mammee apple tree ends up, every year, as ice cream. The Key West Firehouse Museum holds an annual mamey ice cream social, made with fruit from the tree in its yard, and in June 2024 the tree was still bearing.

It is the state champion of its species on the Florida Forest Service register. In 2018 the county forester measured it at 328 centimetres round at chest height and 14.9 metres tall, with a crown about 17 by 12 metres. He also wrote down its condition: fair, mature and declining. The 2024 fruit is the most recent word on its health.

Nobody recorded when it went in. Firehouse No. 3 was built in 1908, and the museum's account is that the tree followed a few years later. Volunteers threw it a 105th birthday party in 2019, a date worked back from the roughly 21 years a mamey needs before it fruits; a 2024 newspaper caption made it 115. Both are the museum's guess, so call it somewhere between 100 and 120.

One naming trap: "mamey" is also the common name of Pouteria sapota, a different species altogether. The register is specific that this one is Mammea americana.

The tree stands on city land between the museum and the building next door. The museum is free, with a suggested donation, and opens Wednesday to Saturday from 10:00 to 14:00. Whether you can see the crown from the street without going in, we have not been able to confirm.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the state champion mamey in the museum's yard. It stands between the Key West Firehouse Museum and the building next door, at the corner of Grinnell and Virginia streets.

trees.story:
Key West's own urban foresters have asked to cut these two trees down. The strangler figs in the city cemetery have grown so deep into the graves that the city's forestry report shows them breaking slabs and engulfing headstones, and in November 2025 removing both went on the Tree Commission's agenda.

The report, by Brett Mayle and Zach Bentley of the city's urban forestry team, measured them at 96 and 53 inches across, about 2.4 and 1.35 metres. Worked out as a circle, which a strangler fig's trunk never quite is, the larger comes to roughly 7.7 metres round. It does not say how high up the trunk the tape went.

The local paper calls them over a century old; there is no planting date. The cemetery was founded in 1847, after the hurricane of 1846, and a resident wrote to the commission that most of the graves beneath the figs date from the 1880s.

Residents wrote in against it.The November meeting was cancelled for lack of a quorum, and by February 2026 city staff had asked for the decision to be postponed indefinitely. That is the last word we have found: no vote, and the figs still standing among the stones.

No source names the species, so we give only the genus, and none says where in the 19-acre cemetery they stand, or how far apart. Our pin is the cemetery's middle, in Old Town. Entry is free. If you find them, tell us where.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by what they are doing to the graves: two strangler figs grown into the headstones, the larger about 2.4 metres across. They stand somewhere inside the Key West Cemetery in Old Town.

trees.name: The Kapok Tree

location.address: Whitehead Street at Jackson Square (marked 502 Whitehead St), Key West, FL 33040

trees.story:
The trunk of the Kapok Tree on Whitehead Street measures more than 30 feet around, and with its buttresses that figure is a floor, not a ceiling. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square beside Monroe County's historic courthouse, and a white sign marks the spot, in case the size does not.

Its birth year depends on who you ask. WLRN, reporting in 2024, says a kapok was planted at Jackson Square in 1900. Another account puts the planting at 1905, but we could not read that survey ourselves, so treat those five years as an open question. Either way, the Florida Keys tourism board's estimate of more than a hundred years holds.

It has spent that century next to the county's courthouse. When WLRN reported on the work to harden the old building against hurricanes, it noted that the construction would not disturb the tree. The station also says it draws people in for photographs every day, and the tourism board calls it one of the country's most famous kapoks.

Come in spring or summer and the crown carries pink and white flowers. The rest of the year the trunk does the talking on its own. If you know for certain whether it went into the ground in 1900 or 1905, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the buttressed trunk, more than 30 feet round, and the white sign that marks it. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square, beside the courthouse on Whitehead Street.
trees.access: Free, street-side lawn on Whitehead Street beside the courthouse; a white sign marks the spot.
trees.verify_notes: Pin: OSM natural=tree node 9395545457 named 'The Kapok Tree' (24.5547564,-81.8038174); the OSM address point 502 Whitehead St sits about 40 m north, so the pin is the tree node, not the address. Age: WLRN (2024-04-01, courthouse hardening story) says 'In 1900, a kapok tree was planted at Jackson Square. The giant, beautiful tree still stands today and draws people in for photos daily' and that it will not be disturbed by construction. Florida Keys tourism board (Whitehead Street walk page): trunk circumference 'more than 30 feet' (girth_cm 914 is that figure, a lower bound; buttressed trunk), 'estimated to be more than 100 years old', 'one of the country's most famous Kapok trees', pink and white flowers spring and summer, a sign marks the spot. A search summary claimed a 2018 survey dates it 1905; that PDF (williamvdavidson.com, The Kapoks of Key West 2018) could not be read, so it is NOT used; 1900 vs 1905 is an unresolved possible discrepancy. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-11-10 at the pin (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/414403808). Two sources plus OSM. Same walk as kyw_004 (about 250 m).

trees.name: The Cosgrove House Banyan

location.address: 323 Whitehead Street (front yard of the Cosgrove House, Banyan Resort), Key West, FL 33040

location_site.name: Cosgrove House front yard, 323 Whitehead St

trees.story:
A captain's wife planted this banyan for shade, and a century later it overshadows her house. Myrtle Cosgrove, wife of Captain Cosgrove, put it in the front yard of 323 Whitehead Street in the early 1900s, at a time when Key West was not lush and fresh water came out of cisterns.

The Key West Historic Marker Tour says without softening that the Cosgrove House is literally overshadowed by a landscaping decision she made a hundred years ago. The Banyan Resort, which owns the house today, tells the same story of the planting on its own history page, and adds that this is one of two expansive banyans on the property. The other, which the resort calls the largest, grows in the gardens behind, out of sight from the street.

Neither source names the species beyond banyan, a strangling fig of the genus Ficus, so that is how we list it. Nobody has published its girth or its height either. If you have measured it, or know which fig it is, tell us.

This one is a tree to look at, not to walk under. The yard belongs to a private hotel, so stand on the public sidewalk of Whitehead Street and look in rather than stepping onto the grounds. The Kapok Tree at Jackson Square is about 250 metres away, which makes the two an easy pair on one short walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the banyan in the front yard of the Cosgrove House, 323 Whitehead Street, seen from the public sidewalk. The resort's larger banyan stands in the back gardens, out of view.
trees.access: View-only from the public sidewalk on Whitehead Street; the yard belongs to the Banyan Resort, a private hotel. Do not enter the property.
trees.verify_notes: Age: Key West Historic Marker Tour (marker at 323 Whitehead, page copyright 2018): the house is 'literally overshadowed by a landscaping decision Myrtle Cosgrove, the Captain's wife, made a century ago'; she planted a banyan for shade when Key West was not lush and fresh water came from cisterns. The Banyan Resort's own history page: the front yard contains 'one of the two expansive Banyan Trees on this property which was planted in the early 1900s by Captain Cosgrove's wife, Myrtle'; a second, 'the largest Banyan Tree on the property', stands in the gardens behind (not assessed). The two sources agree on planting by Myrtle Cosgrove in the early 1900s (the resort is the owner of the ground; the marker tour is independent). Species given only as 'banyan' (a strangling fig, genus Ficus), not narrowed. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-05-31 near the address (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/367213402). Pin is the OSM address point for 323 Whitehead, not the trunk; stays approximate; small-site rule (hotel front yard seen from the street). No girth or height found. About 250 m from the Kapok Tree.

trees.name: The Cuban Lignum Vitae

location.address: Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden, 5210 College Road, Stock Island, Key West, FL 33040

location_site.name: Boardwalk area, Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden

trees.story:
Florida's champion Cuban lignum vitae stands 5.8 metres tall and 76 centimetres round. On the state's champion tree register, no tree of its species in Florida scores higher.

The Florida Forest Service measured it on 27 February 2018 in the Boardwalk area of the Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden on Stock Island. The record reads 30 inches round, 19 feet tall, a crown 22 by 21 feet across, 54 points in all. The garden captions it State Champion.

That measurement came five months after Hurricane Irma. In September 2017 the storm destroyed the garden's champion pigeon plum and knocked down three other champions. On the garden's own list of its record trees after the storm, this one is marked OK.

One naming trap. The garden also grows another lignum vitae, Guaiacum sanctum, in its general collection. This is Guaiacum officinale, and the register names it so.

Nobody has published when it was planted. The garden began in 1936 as a Works Progress Administration project, but no source puts this tree in that first planting, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

It grows about seven metres from the garden's Barringtonia, another tree on the state register, so the two make one stop on the boardwalk. Adults pay $15, seniors $10, and children 12 and under go free. The garden opens daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., closes on Christmas Day and New Year's Day, and parking is free.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the shorter of two register trees about 7 metres apart in the garden's Boardwalk area, 5.8 metres tall and 76 cm round. The other, a Barringtonia, stands 9.1 metres tall.

Free parking. The tree stands in the Boardwalk area of the garden.

trees.name: The Boardwalk Barringtonia

location.address: Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden, 5210 College Road, Stock Island, Key West, FL 33040

location_site.name: Boardwalk area, Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden

trees.story:
Whether this tree is still Florida's champion depends on whose list you read. The Florida Forest Service register has it as the state's champion Barringtonia asiatica. The Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden, which owns the ground it grows in, files it under Historic Legacy Trees and calls it a former champion.

The register's numbers date from 27 February 2018, when the tree stood 30 feet tall, 30 inches round, a crown 26 by 21 feet across, 66 points in all. The garden does not say when it lost the title, and we have not found a newer measurement, so we give you both lists and no verdict.

It has at least outlasted a hurricane. Irma went through in September 2017, destroyed the garden's champion pigeon plum and knocked down three other champions. On the garden's list after the storm, this one is marked OK.

Nobody has recorded its age. The garden started in 1936 as a Works Progress Administration project, but no source puts this tree in that planting. If you know when it went in, tell us.

It grows in the Boardwalk area on Stock Island, about seven metres from the garden's Cuban lignum vitae, Florida's champion of that species, so one stop covers both. Adults pay $15, seniors $10, and children 12 and under go free. The garden opens daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., closes on Christmas Day and New Year's Day, and parking is free.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the taller of two register trees about 7 metres apart in the garden's Boardwalk area, 9.1 metres tall and 76 cm round. The shorter one beside it, 5.8 metres, is the Cuban lignum vitae.

Free parking. The tree stands in the Boardwalk area of the garden.

trees.name: The Elephant-Foot Kapok

location.address: Old Town, Key West, Florida (the reader's GPS fix)

trees.how_to_recognise: A smooth grey kapok whose roots spill over the ground in great rounded humps like an elephant's foot, its trunk ringed with knobbly swellings where the lower limbs leave it.
trees.access: The reader photographed it from the path beside it. We have not confirmed whose ground it stands on; look from the path.
trees.story:
Key West has a soft spot for its kapoks, and this reader, who had already sent us the one at the courthouse, kept going and found another in Old Town, a few hundred metres from the city cemetery, with a GPS fix taken at its foot.

The photograph is all trunk. The bark is the smooth elephant grey of an old kapok, and at the bottom the roots do not so much go into the ground as pour out over it, in huge rounded humps and ridges that spread several metres before they disappear, so that the whole base looks like a giant animal's foot set down on the path. Higher up the trunk is ringed with knobbly collars where limbs leave it, and the limbs themselves run almost level before they turn up into a canopy of fingered leaves. A flame tree in flower hangs in from the left.

Kapoks come from the tropical Americas and West Africa and grow fast, so a trunk like this need not be very old, but we have no planting date or girth for it. If you know this tree, tell us and we will add it as yours.

Walk round the base slowly; the roots change shape on every side.

trees.name: The White Street Kapoks

location.address: Beside Key West City Hall, 1300 White Street, Key West, Florida

trees.how_to_recognise: In the planted bed beside the cream building with white shutters: a kapok whose buttress roots twist up around the trunk like ropes, a second big kapok standing just behind it.
trees.access: Free. In a planted bed beside a public building, seen from the paths around it.
verified_sources: https://keysweekly.com/?p=71201 (Keys Weekly: the 1923 school building at 1300 White Street is now Key West City Hall)
trees.story:
The reader who sent this one called it "Even More Key West Kapoks", and the plural is fair: there are two of them, one behind the other, beside the cream building with white shutters on White Street where the reader's GPS fix puts them. That building opened as Key West's high school in 1923 and is now City Hall.

The nearer tree is the one to look at. Its roots rise out of the bed in long twisting ribs that wrap around the trunk as they climb, as if the tree were wringing itself out, and one of them peels away from the rest to make a deep hollow at the foot. Above, the smooth grey trunk opens into heavy limbs with knobbly bosses where branches have come off, carrying a broad canopy of fingered leaves that shades the steps and the bike racks. The second kapok, which the reader photographed too, stands a few metres back with the same pale bark.

We have no planting date or girth for either. If you know when they went in, perhaps in the school's day, tell us and we will add it as yours.

Stand by the steps to see both trunks in line.
